posts:
HR launched an inter-department tournament. By week three, two departments out of ten were still playing.

This is not about interest in football. This is how most workplace tournaments are built.

What actually breaks:

Week 1. Enthusiasm.

Everyone signs up, the chat is busy, someone buys kit. HR keeps the schedule in a spreadsheet and sends it round personally.

It all works, because HR is working.

Week 2. The questions start.

"When do we play?" — eight times in the group chat.
"Who is top?" — nobody knows, only HR has seen the table.
"Are we out?" — no quick answer exists.

HR replies to everyone individually. That takes more time than organising did.

Week 3. Silence.

HR is on leave. The schedule was not updated. Two departments who remembered their fixture played it. Everyone else assumed the thing was over.

Officially it is still running. In practice it is not.

The real cause here.

Not lack of interest. Not busy employees.

The fact that every piece of information lived in one person's head and DMs. They stepped out of the process, the process stopped.

What changes it:

— One permanent link to schedule and table, posted once
— A second person with edit rights
— A season of one evening a week rather than a single off-site day

Six weeks of evenings engages far better than one Saturday.

And what stays with HR regardless: the venue, the referee and the prizes. No system does those for you.

HR people — was your last tournament run by one person or by a group? Be honest.
